newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms lag U.S. rivals on shareholder value.
newsitem.headline: German firms lag U.S. rivals on shareholder value.

text.p: Despite their recent conversion to the cult of shareholder value, German firms lag sharply behind their international rivals when it comes to investor returns, according to data presented this week.

A 10-year-old investment in a top German firm yields a paltry premium compared with a similar investment in a typical American blue chip, U.S. shareholder value expert Alfred Rappaport told an investor relations conference here.

Rappaport, credited as the founder of the shareholder value concept, has calculated that only six of Germany's top 15 firms could today deliver 15,000 marks or more on a 10,000-mark investment made in 1986.
By contrast, a $10,000 investment in one of the top 15 U.S. firms would today yield between $24,154 (General Motors ) and $131,404 (Coca Cola ).
Moreover, anyone invested in Deutsche Bank AG, Commerzbank AG, Dresdner Bank AG or the country's biggest industrial group, Daimler-Benz AG had incurred hefty losses in the last 10 years.
In the U.S., by contrast, the only loss-making investors would be those who bought IBM shares, a $10,000 package of which has declined in value to $8,326.

German executives attending the conference accepted that more efforts were needed to reward investors, although some blamed German legal restrictions for hampering their efforts to create more value for stockholders.

Juergen Krumnow, board member at Deutsche Bank, said the bank would happily respond to calls from the international investment community to offload some of its valuable industrial holdings, but fiscal restrictions prevented it from doing so.
"The fact that the taxman would get 60 percent of the hidden reserves revealed in that process forbids it," he said.

Deutsche, long criticised for being secretive and holding too large a proportion of undisclosed reserves, is among the most prominent of German companies to embrace shareholder value and last year for the first time reported accounts according to International Accounting Standards.

Nonetheless, a 10,000 mark investment in 1986 in Deutsche, the country's largest commercial bank, would yield only 7,510 marks today, just slightly more than the 7,466-mark return on a comparable investment in Daimler, according to Rappaport.
The giant engineering group Siemens AG is doing somewhat better, with a theoretical 10,000 mark investment in 1986 now worth a more respectable 10,384 marks.

Edgar Wittmann, strategy executive at the giant electronics and engineering group, noted that Siemens had made substantial efforts to improve its value but said the group wanted to take more aggressive steps in future to clean up its corporate shareholdings in particular.
However Robert Koehler, chief executive of one of the darlings of the German stock exchange, SGL Carbon, said most German firms lacked commitment to shareholder value.
Boosting value is a priority for SGL, whose share price has doubled in the last 18 months, Koehler said.

But in general, "chief financial officers have some understanding of shareholder value, the (other) board members have different views on whether to pay it any attention and marketing managers are not even in the picture," said Koehler.
However Rappaport himself was less pessimistic, pointing out that only 10 percent of the top 500 U.S. firms had implemented shareholder value initiatives, giving Germany a good chance of catching up.
German economics professor Rolf Buehner said shareholder value concepts, already a hot topic in Germany, would spread even further in the years to come.
"The train has only just started to roll," he said.
